title: Addressable Memory for Video World Models
claim: A baseline cache fails to reproduce the initial scene after a long loop trajectory; ours recovers it faithfully.
layout: Camera-path diagram left, 2x5 frame grid right, rows contrast baseline versus ours
description: The figure has two parts. On the left, a rounded panel titled 'Camera path' shows a tilted grid floor with camera icons at four waypoints A (start), B, C and D, connected by arrows labeled Forward, Right, Backward and Left. The path text below reads A → B → C → D → A. On the right is a 2x5 grid of forest-scene video frames. Columns are Start A, Waypoint B, Waypoint C, Waypoint D and Return A. The top row is the sliding-window baseline, and the bottom row is WorldTrace (ours). Coordinates and timesteps (t = 0 to 16) sit below the columns. The start frames have blue borders. The baseline's return frame has a red border and is labeled 'incorrect', because it shows a different scene. Our return frame has a green border and is labeled 'correct', because it matches the start. The eye goes first to the red and green return frames at the right.
caption: Addressable memory maintains long-horizon visual persistence. (Left) Loop topology A$\to$B$\to$C$\to$D$\to$A. (Right) Representative frames on Matrix-Game-2 along the path, covering the initial scene A (blue border), waypoints B, C, and D, and the return to A. Sliding window (top) mismatches the reference appearance at the return (red border). Our \worldtrace with frozen landmark keys (green border) matches scene A at the return.
abstract: We study visual persistence in interactive video world models. These models rely on a Key-Value (KV) cache as a growing visual memory to carry forward previously generated frames. However, we find that models can no longer reliably address stored content once rollouts extend beyond the training horizon, because temporal Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) offsets can exceed the training range and the model struggles to retrieve the relevant visual information through attention. Moreover, naively compressing the cache in the RoPE-rotated space degrades memory by averaging keys with incompatible positional phases. To address this, we propose WorldTrace, a training-free memory framework for long-horizon visual persistence. WorldTrace keeps compressed memory addressable by assigning each summary slot a distinct, in-distribution virtual position. Within this cache, WorldTrace uses the model's own attention to decide which observations to retain verbatim and which redundant ones to merge into compressed summaries, all within one bounded addressable memory bank. We evaluate this ability with LoopBench, a benchmark that tests whether a compressed cache can reconstruct a previously visited scene after a long detour. On LoopBench, WorldTrace improves average DINOv2 recall similarity by 32.6% over a sliding window at the same cache budget, extending visually persistent generation without retraining.
